en: The General Meaning of *Śamatha* and *Vipaśyanā*,
composed by the Tiantai Śramaṇa Shi Zhanran of the Tang Dynasty.
In response to the request of Yuanwai Li Hua to know the general meaning of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*, I briefly report these essential outlines.
This is a brief outline of the general framework of the gates of teaching and contemplation.
In the present school of the family (Huiwen), Nāgārjuna is regarded as the founding patriarch;
however, Huiwen merely enumerates internal contemplation regarding seeing and hearing.
Reaching the Southern Peak and Tiantai,
he further developed *dhāraṇī* through the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-samādhi*.
In his pioneering work on the contemplation of the Dharma-gate, he was thoroughly comprehensive;
in his exegesis of the various sutras,
he consistently employed the fivefold profound interpretation of the ten meanings.
The contemplation of the interpenetration of phenomena employs the expedient means of the five categories and the practice of the ten vehicles.
Regarding these five stages:
Regarding the five profound meanings preceding all sutras:
their names are common while their meanings differ;
thus, the general is used to encompass the particular.
That is to say: explaining the names,
establishing the substance,
and clarifying the central tenet.
Discerning the functions and judging the teachings:
from before the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* onward, the various teachings had not yet been harmonized; all five stages were still coarse.
Coming to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, both the name and the substance are wondrous;
this is explained in detail as in the ten volumes of the *Xuánwén*.
Regarding what are called the "ten meanings":
First, it clarifies that the principle is quiescent and absolute, transcending all departure and being inconceivable;
within this single quiescent principle, which is undivided yet divided,
one departs from and opens up all the truths (*satya*).
That is to say, the fourfold Four Truths, the sevenfold Two Truths, the fivefold Three Truths, and so forth.
Whether expanded or condensed, the principles of the provisional and the ultimate are clearly visible.
Second, the teaching gates that express these meanings.
The structural framework stands firm, encompassing both the esoteric and the exoteric;
this refers to the eight categories: gradual, sudden, indeterminate, secret, treasury, common, distinct, and perfect.
One who attains these eight meanings [understands the teaching].
The way in which the teachings of the One Vehicle’s voice transform beings can thus be known.
In the three [traditions], the scriptures and treatises contradict one another and their verbal meanings are mutually inconsistent;
they cannot be reconciled through mere sentiment.
This cannot be understood through mere extensive erudition.
From antiquity until the present day, those who cling to their own views have debated without ceasing for generations.
Now, I shall employ the intent of the four *siddhāntas*.
Fourth, skillfully destroying attachment:
there is no stagnation and nothing that is not integrated; one exerts oneself with sovereign mastery.
Skillfully employing various phrases to shatter the mind that clings,
one pursues the delusions to be destroyed— whether they be single, multiple, or complete—
until they are exhausted beyond words.
The fifth is the Dharma-gate of the Correct Binding.
It corresponds to the stages of practice so that one may cultivate according to the teachings with skillful means;
it establishes gradations for realization based on practice.
The noble and holy do not err;
they are thus freed from overweening pride.
Sixth, they follow a single phrase with unimpeded mastery whether applied horizontally or vertically.
Yet the threads of the text follow one another in sequence, forming a complete and elegant composition.
The seven opening chapters and their topical divisions are linked like interlocking hooks,
decisively elucidating the momentum of the prose and providing the structural framework for its unfolding.
Eighth, the exegesis of the scriptural text must accord with its meaning and conform to reason.
Ninth, the translation of local dialects.
This ensures that names and meanings are not obstructed.
Eleventh, beneath each phrase, one employs rational contemplation to dissolve and penetrate [the meaning];
this accords with the sutras, seals the mind, and establishes practice.
Do not waste your time on the treasures of others.
If you would explain the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, you must first thoroughly understand the provisional and the real, as well as the fundamental and the manifested;
only then can you establish your practice.
This sutra alone is uniquely entitled "Wondrous";
only by relying upon it can one establish the intent of contemplation.
As for the statement regarding the five expedient means and the ten stages of practice:
This Sudden and Perfect Calming and Contemplation is entirely based upon the Perfect and Sudden Calming and Contemplation of the Lotus Sutra;
it is merely another name for the Lotus Samādhi.
If one wishes to practice this Perfect and Sudden Samādhi:
To be fully endowed with the ten stages of the vehicle is called "perfect practice.
Although the dharma-texts of the "Expedient Means" chapter are brief,
they are sufficient through the parable of the great carriage in the "Parable" chapter.
However, the ten-fascicle *Śamatha-vipaśyanā* is broadly divided into two parts:
the first two fascicles provide a concise explanation of the fundamental framework,
while the subsequent eight fascicles extensively clarify the specific modes of practice.
The initial brief explanation is further divided into five parts:
namely, generating the perfect mind and cultivating the perfect practice.
Experiencing the perfect fruit,
he gives rise to the eight teachings to return to the three virtues;
the initial arousal of the perfect mind occurs in the first fascicle.
This means that by means of the four great vows, the four noble truths,
and the six stages of realization, one distinguishes the characteristics of partial and perfect resolve.
The four great vows are the vows that initiate this resolve.
The Four Truths are the objective realm upon which one relies;
the six [perfections] are the stages traversed.
If a vow lacks an objective realm, it is called a deluded aspiration.
If the objective realm is not distinguished by stage, there is no differentiation between ordinary beings and sages.
To say that the vow is generated based on the objective realm means:
"I vow to deliver infinite sentient beings."
Relying on the objective realm of the truth of suffering (*duḥkha-satya*),
he vows to sever countless afflictions (*kleśa*).
Relying on the objective realm of the truth of origination (*samudaya-satya*)...
"I vow to know the inexhaustible Dharma gates," based on the objective realm of the Truth of the Path;
"I vow to accomplish the unsurpassed Buddha-way," based on the objective realm of the Truth of Cessation.
In the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, the Four Noble Truths are expanded into four stages;
consequently, the great vows are likewise presented in four iterations.
Here, we select the partial for the sake of the perfect.
By means of this perfect fourth vow, the previous three vows are integrated;
since there is nothing that is not the Dharma-realm (dharmadhātu),
one gives rise to sublime vows based upon the Dharma-realm.
The initial mind universally encompasses the contemplation of the dharma-realm of afflictions;
it universally practices the Buddha-dharmas and realizes the three bodies and so forth.
Having already given rise to the perfect mind, one may not yet fully know the perfect mind.
Is it the initial mind that is this?
Is it the subsequent mind that is this?
Or is it that the initial [mind] is itself the subsequent?
The beginning is different from the end.
If the beginning is not the end, and if the initial mind is different from the subsequent one.
Since neither [of these] is perfectly interfused,
one distinguishes the six stages of "thusness" (liu ji) to determine what is correct and what is erroneous;
namely, the stage of "principle thusness" (li ji).
The name-stage,
the contemplative practice stage,
and the semblance stage.
The partial realization of suchness and the ultimate realization of suchness: because they are identical,
both the beginning and the end are [the same].
Thus, because there are six [factors], the first and the last are not confused;
because their principle is the same, they are identical,
yet because their phenomena differ, they are six.
In all the sutras, whenever there are instances where something is identified as being identical to another—
such as the category of "birth-and-death is itself nirvana"—
these are all distinguished by means of the six positions.
This ensures that the principle remains consistent from beginning to end,
so that there is no confusion between the initial and subsequent stages.
Next are the four passages concerning the cultivation of the perfect practice (*paripūrṇa-caryā*) and so forth.
Furthermore, in the second fascicle,
regarding the "initially perfected practitioner," it refers to the four types of samādhi which universally encompass all practices.
If there were no superior practice, it would be difficult to attain the superior fruit.
The *Ekāsanika* (One Who Always Sits) is described in both the *Mañjuśrīparipṛcchā-sūtra* and the *Mañjuśrībuddhakṣetraguṇavyūha-sūtra*,
and is also called the *Ekākārasamādhi* (Samādhi of a Single Practice).
It is solely because of single-minded mindfulness of the *dharmadhātu*.
One should take a period of ninety days as one session.
Second, one should constantly practice the *Pratyutpanna-samādhi Sūtra*.
It is also called the Buddha-standing Samādhi.
When it is accomplished, one sees the Buddhas of the ten directions standing within the chamber.
It is also practiced for a single period of ninety days.
Third, the methods for emerging from half-walking and half-sitting meditation according to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* and the *Vaipulya* sūtras:
in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, a period of twenty-one days constitutes one cycle;
in the *Vaipulya* sūtras, there is no restriction on the duration of time.
The fourth, neither walking nor sitting, is also called "following one's own intention," because one contemplates as soon as the intention arises.
Its methods are derived from various Mahāyāna sūtras such as the *Avalokiteśvara-vikurvaṇa-nirdeśa*.
These may also be practiced during the four modes of deportment and amidst various tasks, whether public or private,
and even in moments of haste or urgency.
These four samādhis differ in their practice but are identical in principle.
Therefore, they equally employ the method of the ten stages.
As for the second point, "attaining the perfect fruit":
it is by means of these various practices that one enters the stage of perfection.
Proximately, that which is attained at the first stage is called the Patience of Non-arising (*anutpattika-dharmakṣānti*);
distantly, that which is aimed for at the stage of Wondrous Enlightenment is called the Patience of Quiescent Extinction (*śānta-nirodha-kṣānti*).
The functional capacities of the first stage are fully described in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*’s eulogy of the first stage.
This is precisely its characteristic.
How could one hastily claim to have realized the truth?
This extends even to the stage of wondrous enlightenment, as explained at length in the sutras.
Regarding the "three arisings and eight teachings":
having already entered the [bodhisattva] stages, one accomplishes the path through the eight phases and manifests bodies for the ten realms.
Being able to accord with the capacities of sentient beings,
[the Buddha] employed the four methods such as the Tripitaka and the four approaches such as the gradual,
benefiting beings throughout five periods.
Regarding the beginning and end of a single lifetime:
as for the four returns to the three virtues,
once the conditions of the capacity [of sentient beings] have ceased, one should appropriately return to the three virtues.
What are the three virtues?
They are called the Secret Treasury.
Thus, the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* says:
I have placed my children within the secret treasury,
and I too shall not long remain outside it, but shall enter therein myself.
Thus ends the third fascicle.
The aspects of practice are explained in detail,
elaborating upon the first five so that they may be easily practiced.
This refers to: explaining the names of śamatha and vipaśyanā;
discerning the essence of śamatha and vipaśyanā;
and clarifying how their essence encompasses all phenomena.
The judgment of the partial and the perfect regarding these four [teachings] is all contained within the third fascicle.
Next, for the sake of correct cultivation, the preparatory practices (*pūrvaprayoga*) are all contained within the fourth fascicle.
That is to say, there are twenty-five factors,
which are collectively organized into five sections;
the first consists of five conditions.
First, clothing and food are fully provided,
because one is free from the conditions of longing;
second, the precepts are pure.
Because it abandons the causes for rebirth in the evil realms;
and because, in the third [stage], one dwells in secluded and quiet places,
abandoning the affairs of clamor and bustle.
Fourth, one must cease all worldly affairs and abandon base and miscellaneous occupations.
Fifth, one must rely on a spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra) who serves as a ground for consultation and inquiry.
Within each passage, there are two aspects: the phenomenal and the principle.
Second is the censure of the five desires, namely:
form, sound, fragrance, taste, and touch.
Both the primary retribution and the secondary environment each possess these five [aspects],
and they are all capable of giving rise to the practitioner’s desire for what is needed; therefore,
they must be reviled and extinguished.
Within the text itself, there are two types of censure: that concerning phenomena and that concerning principles.
Regarding the "abandonment of the three and the five hindrances":
only when the necessary conditions are fulfilled and desire is absent is one capable of entering meditative contemplation.
One contemplates the five factors that obscure the mind when it has not yet attained meditative equipoise—
namely, sensual desire, ill will, sloth and torpor, restlessness and remorse, and doubt.
Because these arise through contemplation, they are significantly different from their ordinary manifestations.
Once one has realized that which harms tranquil illumination, it must be abandoned;
within the text, there are two types of abandonment for each: that of phenomena and that of principle.
Regarding the four adjustments and five matters:
This is because one does not enter [the state].
It is because these five factors—the body and so forth—are not harmonized.
That is to say, the body, breath, mind, and the three concentrations must be internally and harmoniously integrated.
Ensure that the body is neither too loose nor too tight;
let the mind be free from both harshness and laxity, and free from both agitation and depression.
Regarding the two dharmas of sleep and food, each must be regulated according to the prescribed rules.
One should not be irregular in sleep nor excessive in eating;
one should ensure that one is neither hungry nor satiated.
As for the five practices and five dharmas:
Although the four categories are complete, these five must necessarily constitute the beginning of practice.
First is aspiration (*chanda*),
for it is necessary to have a longing [for the goal].
Second is single-minded mindfulness,
because one must maintain it through recollection;
third is diligence.
The four analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*) are required because of the need for continuity; the four skillful means (*kauśalya*) are required because of the need for transformation.
5. One-pointedness of mind.
Because there is no seeking of anything else, one possesses this skillful means.
Right contemplation can be attained.
What is right contemplation?
It refers to the ten dharmas.
If these ten are absent,
it is called a "ruined donkey-cart.
Furthermore, although these ten factors are all complete and constant, they are [only] complete in their totality.
Furthermore, there are three types of faculties among persons that are unequal:
those of superior faculty possess only one dharma;
those of middling faculty possess either two or seven.
Those of inferior capacity must first complete all ten;
those of superior capacity practice a single dharma,
which is the contemplation of the inconceivable realm.
The object is that which is observed;
the observation is that which observes.
What is the object of observation?
That is to say, the aggregates (skandhas), elements (dhātus), and sense-bases (āyatanas) do not transcend matter and mind.
Matter is constructed from the mind; its entire substance is mind.
Therefore, a sutra says:
In the three realms there are no separate dharmas;
they are created solely by this one mind.
This creative capacity is fully endowed with all phenomena.
Whether they be outflows (*āsrava*), non-outflows, or neither outflows nor non-outflows;
whether they be causes, effects, or neither cause nor effect—
and so forth— therefore the Sūtra says:
Mind, Buddha, and sentient beings—
these three are without distinction.
The principle that all sentient beings inherently possess the state of being already perfected as Buddhas.
The phenomena and their underlying principles are equal in nature;
that is to say, within each and every mind there are all minds,
and within each and every object there are all objects.
Within each and every mind are all atoms;
within each and every atom are all minds;
within each and every atom are all lands.
So it is with all atoms of all lands;
the bodies of all dharmas, all atoms,
and all lands are perfectly complete in essence, yet devoid of intrinsic nature.
Non-substantiality is inherently subject to transformation according to objects;
thus, the mutual interpenetration of phenomena is ever-present.
Therefore, my body and mind pervade the dust motes within every world-system.
So it is with all Buddhas and sentient beings: the essence of each individual body and land is eternally identical.
What prevents the mind, the Buddha, and sentient beings from being one?
Because they are distinct, they differentiate between the conditions of defilement and purity.
The essence of conditions is fundamentally empty, yet emptiness is not empty.
The three truths, the three contemplations, and the three that are not three—
three, one, and one-three have no place of reliance.
Contemplate carefully that while the names are distinct, their essence is the same;

therefore, the duality of subject and object is neither two nor three. The meaning of the "three contemplations" (san guan) is found in the *Śrī-mālā-siṃhanāda-sūtra* and other scriptures, while the meaning of the "three truths" (san di) is found in the *Rājāvavādaka-sūtra* and other scriptures.
When contemplating in this manner, it is called contemplating the nature of the mind (*cittatva*).
Because it remains unchanging while following conditions, it is called "nature" (prakṛti).
Because it follows conditions while remaining unchanging, it is called "mind" (citta).
Thus, the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* says:
To be able to contemplate the nature of the mind is called the supreme concentration.
The supreme concentration is termed the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).
The primary meaning is called Buddha-nature.
As for Buddha-nature:
He is named Vairocana.
This nature of Vairocana is endowed with the three Buddha-natures;
because Vairocana is all-pervasive, the three Buddha-natures are likewise all-pervasive.
Therefore, know that the three Buddhas are but a single moment.
Since the three Buddhas are all-pervasive, the moment is likewise all-pervasive.
One who contemplates in this manner—
This is called the contemplation of afflictions;
it is called the contemplation of the Dharma-body.
This is the contemplation of the Dharma-body.
This is the contemplation of the three bodies;
this is the contemplation of the moment;
this is the contemplation of the ocean-treasury.
This is the contemplation of True Suchness;
this is the contemplation of the Real Mark;
this is the contemplation of sentient beings.
This is the contemplation of one's own body;
this is the contemplation of empty space; this is the contemplation of the Middle Way.
Therefore, this wondrous realm is the foundation of all dharmas.
Therefore, this wondrous contemplation is the source of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*).
Only in this way can one depart from the biased, the limited, the heterodox, and the external;
for this reason, it stands at the head of the ten dharmas.
For those of superior faculties, a single contemplation— encompassing both the horizontal and vertical dimensions—
immediately brings awareness that while there is no-markedness, all marks are vividly present;
thus they shatter ignorance and ascend to the First Abode.
If one is an ordinary person, whether internal or external,

one must once again make a vow.
Within a state of meditative stillness, contemplate yourself and others;
feel the piercing pain of both self and other,
who have been submerged and circling in birth and death for immeasurable eons.
Although I have previously given rise to minor aspirations and become deluded regarding the bodhicitta,

for birth and death are themselves nirvana;

Because afflictions are themselves awakening,
one vows to know the inexhaustible Dharma gates; that is,
because delusions are transformed into wisdom.
Because the unsurpassed Buddha-way is the vow to achieve birth and death simultaneously,
he contemplated this and attained sudden, great enlightenment;
his mind’s illumination reached its ultimate object, and he entered the stages of both ordinary beings and sages.

Because the mind is not at peace.

As for what is called "comprehensive," it takes the dharma-realm as that which is established and tranquil illumination as that which establishes.

Their intrinsic nature is like space.

The essence is the dharma-realm that is the object of peace;
its function is the tranquil illumination that brings about peace.
The essence is named the equal dharma-body.

The essence and its function are neither two nor three; their virtuous principles are equal.

Therefore, we now follow their nature to bring them peace:

according to their inclinations, according to what requires treatment, and according to the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).
Why is this? Because while there are those whose roots of goodness increase through tranquil illumination,
there are also those whose do not increase.

Whether they revolve through hearing and reflection,

First, regarding the foundations of mindfulness:
That is to say, the four dharmas of body, sensation,
mind, and phenomena are all examined through the three truths within the mind of the dharma-nature.
First, regarding the contemplation of the body:
the body is a material phenomenon (*rūpa-dharma*).
One contemplates the nature of phenomena such that the color of one thing is the color of all things.

both illuminating one and all;

Regarding the seventh, the antidotes that assist the path:
the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra* states,
"The afflictions of sentient beings are not of a single kind."
The Buddha has taught immeasurable gates of remedial practice.
One should know that a person who does not believe in the existence of such remedies has not yet understood correct practice.
If one recognizes that one's own conduct is not yet discerning,
it is truly because unwholesome matters assist unwholesome principles,
together obscuring wholesome principles so that they do not manifest.
"Virtue in principle" refers to the eternal abiding of the dharma-realm;
"virtue in phenomena" refers to...
The six [perfections], such as giving,
are the phenomena; the "unwholesome" in terms of principle refers to subtle ignorance.
As for "matters that are evil," this refers to the six heavy obscurations,
which are eliminated through the cultivation of śamatha and vipaśyanā.
These six manifest:
stinginess, greed, breaking the precepts, anger, sloth, and delusion.
To possess these six evils and yet claim that there is a superior Dharma within is a contradiction.
Some say it is eternally self-corresponding.
If it were corresponding, it would be identical to the Dharmakāya;
thus, it would have no fixed location, and its teachings would necessarily accord with the capacities of sentient beings.
If one were to give rise to evil again after having briefly attained such correspondence [with the path], there would be no such principle;
it would then obstruct the attainment of Buddhahood by causing one to revert once more to the state of a sentient being.
If it is said that having once attained realization does not hinder [the occurrence of evil], the same applies here.
If it is said that knowing the principle does not hinder one from committing evil,
then one should likewise know wealth and thereby avoid poverty.
By knowing the medicine, one is spared from illness;
when evil matters are removed,
the principles of goodness become easy to clarify.
I still entreat Your Holiness to grant your sacred assistance in helping me manifest this principle. If it is so,
then simply observing evil is itself the Way.
How could evil be able to obscure principle?
This interpretation is not correct.
If evil has already been perfected as the Way, then that Way is itself the Dharma-body.
Because the Dharmakāya has not yet been realized, one must immediately contemplate the subtle;
first, one cultivates the perfections of phenomena to remedy phenomenal evils.
Once phenomenal evils have been overturned, the goodness of principle can arise.
Therefore, those who cultivate contemplation must examine [their practice] through the reality of evil and judge it by means of the six stages of realization.
When principle is clearly elucidated, phenomena that are evil will inevitably perish.
